newsitem.title: UK: EBRD has reasons to be cheerful at annual meeting.
newsitem.headline: EBRD has reasons to be cheerful at annual meeting.

text.p: Governors of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) have several reasons to be cheerful when they hold their annual meeting in London next week.
The countries of central and eastern Europe, which the EBRD was set up in 1991 to help, are in reasonable economic shape and the bank itself is making a steady operating profit.
There are clouds on the horizon, such as political instability in Albania and question marks over the future of reform in countries such as Bulgaria, Belarus and Ukraine.

But EBRD shareholders are generally happy with the way the bank is developing and no major issues stand out as the agenda for the annual meeting on April 14 and 15 is finalised, says Bart le Blanc, EBRD vice-president for finance.
"If you look back over the last six years and compare achievements so far with the strategy that was set, we have certainly done well," he told Reuters in an interview.
The Bank now has investment projects in all 26 member countries after Tajikistan and Bosnia joined the fold.
Most member countries have achieved a reasonable degree of economic stability after the turmoil that followed the collapse of communism.
"I think the next step in most cases is going to be structural reform," says David Boren, vice-president for economic and market analysis at Salomon Brothers in London.
"Many of the countries are at a fairly advanced stage of the transition, so now the focal point needs to shift to micro reform such as legal infrastructure and tax codes."
Western companies keen to invest in former communist countries complain that their efforts are often hampered by inadequate legal and banking systems and bureaucracy.
They are also keen to see mature domestic capital markets develop in these countries.
The EBRD governors are likely to be concerned about some of the reform "laggards" who have done little to turn themselves into modern market economies.

"There is a second tier of economies which haven't done anything on structural reform and still face major challenges on macro stabilisation, such as the former Soviet republics apart from Russia, Kazakhstan or the Baltics," Boren said.
The EBRD is trying to address this by shifting more of its activities eastwards into the former Soviet republics.
"We are undertaking more investments in countries which are in earlier stages of their reform process, more in the eastern part of the region," le Blanc said.
Russia itself is unlikely to cause any headaches.
"There are no problems about Russia's commitment to reform. It is more a question of implementation and things like tax collection," one EBRD official said.
Financial markets will keep a wary eye on the annual meeting as it will be attended by top officials from the Group of Seven leading industrial nations.
The dollar's recent surge against major currencies has fuelled speculation that governments and central banks may try to intervene on markets to stem its rise.
The EBRD meeting, which will attract a few finance ministers but will mainly be attended by second-rung officials, could provide a forum for informal contacts on market developments.
The annual meeting will be preceded at the weekend by a business forum at which eastern European countries will promote themselves and try to woo foreign investors.
